els.name: summary_heading_and_description.1.summary_description
els.text: Public policies are often designed around expected citizen behavior, but actual behavior can be influenced by many psychological, social, and practical factors. Citizens may understand what a policy asks them to do but still fail to act because of limited information, complicated procedures, lack of attention, habits, social influence, or immediate costs.

els.name: card_content.2.card_description
els.text: Effectiveness asks whether the intervention actually achieved its intended objective and changed the desired behavior.

els.name: card_content.2.card_description
els.text: Efficiency considers whether the desired results were achieved without unnecessary use of public resources such as money, staff time, technology.

els.name: card_content.2.card_description
els.text: Equity asks whether the intervention benefits different groups fairly and whether it creates additional barriers for people who may already have difficulty.

els.name: intro_copy_column.1.description
els.text: A behavioral intervention should not be considered successful simply because it changes people's behavior. Public-sector interventions should be evaluated from three connected perspectives: effectiveness, efficiency, and equity.

els.name: image_card_1.2.card_description
els.text: Governments can test different approaches on a small scale before introducing them more widely. Comparing different versions of a service, message, or intervention helps identify which approach produces better results.

els.name: image_card_2.2.card_description
els.text: Measurable data provides evidence about whether an intervention actually changed behavior. Governments can track indicators such as participation, completion, compliance

els.name: image_card_3.2.card_description
els.text: Evaluation should not be treated as the final step of a policy. Results should be used to improve the intervention and inform future policies.
